t: Number of Ways to Split a String - Count Ones, Then Multiply the Gaps
o:
## Understanding the problem

We split a binary string into three non-empty consecutive parts and need every part to contain the same number of `1` characters, counting the distinct ways modulo 10^9 + 7. The ones-count of each part is fixed once the two cut positions are chosen, so the question is really about where the cuts may slide.

In `10101` the total is 3 ones, so each part needs exactly one. The first cut must sit after the first `1`, the second cut before the last `1`, and the lone middle `1` can be attached to either neighboring part, giving the four combinations listed in the example. In `1001` the total is 2, which is not divisible by 3, so no split exists and the answer is 0. In `0000` there are no ones at all, and any pair of internal gaps works: C(3, 2) = 3 ways.

With length up to 100000, enumerating all cut pairs quadratically is hopeless; a linear scan over a handful of specific one-positions suffices.
k: The split is impossible unless the total number of ones is divisible by 3.
If the string contains no ones, the answer is simply C(n-1, 2): choose two cut points among the n-1 internal gaps.
Otherwise only the neighborhoods of the (total/3)-th and (2*total/3)-th ones matter; the two gap widths multiply to give the count.

a.n: Approach 1: Prefix Sums Over Every Cut Pair
a.i: Build a prefix count of ones, then try every pair of cut positions i < j and keep those where the three parts each hold exactly total/3 ones. This mirrors the definition directly and each check is instant with prefix sums, but there are O(n^2) pairs, which is far too slow at the given limits.
s: Compute pre[i] = number of ones in the first i characters.
Enumerate the first cut i from 1 to n-2.
Enumerate the second cut j from i+1 to n-1.
Accept the pair when pre[i] = pre[j] - pre[i] = total - pre[j].
a.t: O(n^2) - all pairs of cut positions are enumerated with O(1) checks.

a.n: Approach 2: Count Ones and Multiply the Gap Sizes
a.i: Let total be the number of ones. If it is not divisible by three, return 0; if it is zero, return C(n-1, 2). Otherwise locate the (total/3)-th one at position a with its successor b, and the (2*total/3)-th one at c with successor d. The first cut may fall on any gap between a and b, and the second on any gap between c and d, so the answer is (b-a)*(d-c) modulo 10^9 + 7.
s: Count the ones; reject non-multiples of 3 and handle the all-zeros case.
Scan once, recording indices of the k-th, (k+1)-th, (2k)-th and (2k+1)-th ones.
Multiply the two gap widths (b-a) and (d-c).
a.t: O(n) - two passes over the string at most.
a.sp: O(1) - a handful of index variables.

w: Go straight to the counting solution; keep the brute force in your back pocket only as a sanity check on tiny inputs. Pitfalls: skipping the divisibility test, forgetting the all-zeros special case entirely, and overflowing 32-bit integers when multiplying the two gap counts (each up to 1e5, product up to 1e10) in C++ or Java. The modulus applies to the final product only, since intermediate quantities fit comfortably. Likely follow-ups: generalize to splitting an integer array into three parts with equal sums, where prefix sums plus a hash map find the boundary candidates.
